The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston.
The Environmental Protection Agency says testing
is underway in southeast Iowa after the U.S. Army
detonated nearly five tons of hazardous chemicals
at an ammunition plant on Wednesday.
The Army says the controlled explosion was necessary
to prevent dozens of barrels from potentially
exploding on their own.
Eliza Billingham with Iowa Public Radio reports.
The EPA says it has not found any lead in the air
or on the ground in communities surrounding
the Army's detonation zone.
Major General Eric Shirley credits state-of-the-art
mitigation efforts that soldiers put in place
to control the blast.
The lead azide barrels were already underground.
The Army added tarps, gel blocks, and two feet
of particle-collecting foam around the blast zone.
The EPA has roughly 300 people in place to continue
testing air, soil, and surface water for any contamination.
For NPR News, I'm Eliza Billingham in Iowa City.
Judges in Israel are calling to drop some
of the corruption charges against Prime Minister
Benjamin Netanyahu.
The trial against him has been going on for six years,
and he denies wrongdoing.
NPR's Daniel Estrin reports from Tel Aviv.
In a surprise move, the judges overseeing Netanyahu's
corruption trial called on Israel's attorney general
to consider dropping the most serious case of bribery
where Netanyahu was accused of trading business favors
with a media mogul in exchange for positive news coverage.
In the second case involving Netanyahu's dealings
with a newspaper owner, the judges said they doubted
a crime was committed, and the judges recommended
the sides settle the final case where Netanyahu
was accused of getting gifts from a Hollywood producer
and helping him with an Israeli tax break.
This is promising news for Netanyahu,
but he may be unseated as Prime Minister
as early as next week.
His rival, Gadi Eisenkot, is trying to form a new government.
Daniel Estrin, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
The Supreme Court in Puerto Rico says the government
can fire the private company that's been operating
the island's troubled electric grid.
NPR's Adrian Florido says poor infrastructure
has been a long-standing problem for the U.S. territory.
After Hurricane Maria flattened Puerto Rico's power grid
in 2017, the local government brought in a U.S.
and Canada-based firm, Luma Energy, to run it,
rebuild it, and reduce blackouts.
But the grid is still a mess.
Governor Jennifer Gonzalez sued to force Luma out.
Now the island's high court has given her the green light.
The governor said she'll find a new private operator.
Luma Energy has said it's considering its legal options.
It's long said the grid it took over was in awful shape
and that blackouts are not all its fault.
Adrian Florido, NPR News.
This is NPR News.
King tides and powerful surf have torn away part of a pier
just south of San Francisco.
A large wave knocked a section of the pier
into the ocean on Wednesday.
Officials had closed it over the summer
when they found cracks in the structure.
Some beachfront homes in Pacifica are flooding
as the highest tides of the year roll in.
Farther north, officials in Marin County have lifted
an evacuation warning for people living along the waterfront
in Stinson Beach.
Forecasters there expect waves as high
as a three-story building.
The Democratic Republic of Congo says nearly 6,000 people
have died in the country's current outbreak of Ebola.
NPR's Jonathan Lambert says the first vaccines
designed to fight that country's outbreak
are poised to enter a clinical trial.
Regulators in DRC are poised to OK two new Ebola
vaccines for testing.
One is an mRNA vaccine made by Moderna.
The other was developed by the University of Oxford.
In the outbreak's very early days,
both vaccine candidates were fast-tracked
with millions of dollars by a vaccine nonprofit
called the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations.
Researchers are already testing whether an existing Ebola
vaccine designed for a different kind of Ebola
can offer protection.
It'll likely be some time before researchers get any results.
Conducting a clinical trial in this region,
where there's lots of armed conflict, is challenging.
But if the vaccine is effective, it
could help bring the fastest spreading Ebola outbreak ever
to an end.
Jonathan Lambert, NPR News.
This is NPR News in Washington.
